Relative Clauses: Object Pronouns
You use relative clauses to provide extra information about a subject or an object mentioned in a previous clause.

To give additional information about an object, we need to use object relative pronouns such as who, whom, which, and that. We use who, whom, and that for people; and which or that for things.

It’s important not to confuse the subject and object pronouns in the relative clauses; when the relative pronoun is used as a subject pronoun, the main verb goes after it; but when the relative pronoun is used as an object pronoun, there is always a noun or a pronoun after it.

Examples: 

  • This is the manual that covers everything about ASP.NET. (Subject relative pronoun)

  • This is the manual that he gave me, it covers everything about ASP.NET. (Object relative pronoun)

    •  

    Another way to identify object relative pronouns is the fact that they can be omitted from the sentence without changing its meaning:

     

    • This is the manual about ASP.NET that he gave me.
    • This is the manual about ASP.NEThe gave me.

There are two types of clauses: defining and non-defining.  In the defining relative clauses, we add information that is significant to the previous clause while in the non-defining ones the extra information is not relevant.

 

Let's see the grammatical structures below: 

 

Defining Relative Clauses 

Subject + object pronoun + noun or pronoun + complement.



Examples: 

  • The page life cycle which we use to contain various controls is instantiated as a control object.
  • She is the student whom I met in programming class.
  • The app that he created is very interesting.

Non-Defining Relative Clauses

 

Subject, + object pronoun + noun or pronoun+ complement, + other clause.

 

Examples: 

 

  • The professor, who we met yesterday, recommended us a very useful manual.
  • The manual, which he gave me, explained all about the server object. 
  • The page class, which you use, has extremely useful properties.

Thomas: Hi, everybody! I’m Thomas, the person who is going to be in charge of today’s lecture. During this presentation, I will try to explain the most relevant aspects of the Server Object that we use in ASP.NET. First of all, it is quite important to know that this object is an instance of the System.Web.HttpServerUtility class, and it is used to provide functionalities to the server through different properties and methods.

But what do we know about the Server Object properties? Well, there are mainly two properties that this object offers. The first property, which is known as MachineName, is the one you use to get the name of a local computer. The second one is ScripTimeOut which we use for getting and setting the amount of time of a request.

Concerning methods, there are several that are defined by the Server Object. Among them, Server.CreateObject,  Server.Execute, Server.GetLastError, ServerHTMLEncode, Server.MapPath, Server.Transfer and Server.URLEncode.

But what do all these methods do? CreateObject generates an instance of a server component or COM; Execute runs .asp files; GetLastError describes errors conditions, and HTMLEncode turns a specified string into HTML encoding.

Furthermore, we have MapPath, which is the method that we can use when we need to map a specified virtual file path on the server. There is also Transfer, which sends current state information to another web page, and URL encode which applies URL encoding to a specified string.

Finally, you must note that all these methods and properties are only run through the intrinsic Server Object that is provided by ASP.NET.
